abstract: Paternal contribution to early embryogenesis has so far been primarily attributed to sperm alleles, regulatory RNAs and epigenetic modifications. Spermatozoa also carry a complex repertoire of lipids that may influence early embryonic development through structural, metabolic, and signaling functions. Here, we combined in vivo stable isotope labeling with low-input, high-resolution lipidomics to trace the fate of sperm lipids from fertilization to the morula stage in mice. Male mice were metabolically labeled with deuterium oxide (D₂O) throughout spermatogenesis, enabling identification of paternal lipids in embryos by characteristic isotopic mass shifts and MS/MS fragmentation. We found that a selective subset of sperm lipids persists throughout preimplantation development and is enriched in neutral lipids and membrane-associated phospholipids. Fragmentation analysis demonstrated active remodeling of paternal triglycerides within the embryo. Finally, we show that this embryo-persistent paternal lipid cargo is conserved across mice and humans, is dynamically regulated by paternal metabolic status, and is associated with embryonic IGF2/H19 imprinting. Together, these findings identify sperm lipids as a previously unrecognized paternal component that persists in the embryo and may contribute to early embryonic organization and programming.
